blocks.prompt: How a Rocket Pushes
blocks.text: A rocket does not push on the ground. It does not push on the air. A rocket pushes on its own fire. Deep inside, fuel burns and turns into hot gas. The gas rushes out of the bottom of the rocket, very fast. Push the gas down hard, and the gas pushes the rocket up just as hard. That is the whole trick. There is no air in space, so a rocket carries its own air along with its fuel. It brings everything the fire needs. That is why a rocket is so big, and why almost all of it is tank.

blocks.prompt: The Rocket That Throws Itself Away
blocks.text: A rocket has a problem, and the problem is its own weight. Almost everything a rocket needs is fuel. On a big rocket, about nine tenths of the weight sitting on the launch pad is fuel and the tanks that hold it. The people, the satellite, the science gear, all of that is a tiny bit at the very top. As the rocket climbs, it burns through the fuel in the bottom tank. Soon that tank is empty. An empty tank is not useful. It is just heavy metal, and the engines have to drag it along. So the rocket does something clever. It throws the empty part away. Bolts fire, the empty stage falls off, and a fresh engine lights on the smaller rocket that is left. Now the rocket is lighter, so it speeds up faster. Big rockets do this two or three times on the way up. By the time the last piece reaches space, most of the rocket is gone. Engineers call each dropped piece a stage.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The edge of space is about 62 miles up
Orbit speed is about 17,500 miles per hour

blocks.prompt: Why Space Is Not Up
blocks.text: Ask someone where space is and they will point up. That answer is close enough for a conversation, and it is almost useless for a rocket. The official edge of space sits about sixty two miles above your head. That is not far. A car could drive it in an hour, if roads went that way. Rockets have flown straight up, touched that line, and come straight back down again fifteen minutes later. The passengers saw the black sky and the curve of the Earth, and then gravity took them home. Going up is the easy half. Staying is the hard half. To stay in space, you have to go sideways, and you have to go sideways absurdly fast. About seventeen thousand five hundred miles per hour. Newton explained why with a thought experiment about a cannon on a very tall mountain. Fire the cannonball gently and it arcs down and lands. Fire it harder and it lands farther away. Fire it hard enough and the ground curves away beneath it exactly as fast as the ball falls. Now it never lands. It falls forever, all the way around the planet. That is an orbit. Astronauts are not floating because gravity stopped. Gravity up there is nearly as strong as it is in your kitchen. They are falling, constantly, and missing the Earth, constantly, because they are moving sideways so fast. That is why a rocket does not fly straight up. Watch a launch and you will see it lean over almost immediately, tipping toward the horizon. It is not aiming for the sky. It is aiming around the world.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Gunpowder rockets flew in China by the 1200s
Tsiolkovsky published the rocket equation in 1903
Goddard launched the first liquid fuel rocket in 1926
It flew 41 feet in about 2.5 seconds
A rocket works better in a vacuum than in air

blocks.prompt: Nobody Believed Robert Goddard
blocks.text: For most of history, a rocket was a weapon and nothing more. Chinese armies were strapping tubes of gunpowder to arrows by the 1200s, and for the next six hundred years that is roughly what a rocket stayed: a firework with a grudge. It burned, it flew, it landed somewhere, and nobody expected it to be steered or to be useful anywhere but a battlefield. The idea that a rocket could carry a person off the planet belonged to a deaf schoolteacher in a small Russian town. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky taught math in Kaluga and worked out the physics in his spare time. In 1903 he published the equation that still governs every launch: how fast a rocket can go depends on how fast it throws its exhaust, and on how much of the rocket is fuel. From that one line of math he predicted liquid fuel, multiple stages, and space stations. He never built a rocket. He did not need to. The math was the discovery. Building it fell to an American physicist named Robert Goddard. Goddard was quiet, private, and thoroughly mocked. In 1920, after he suggested a rocket could reach the moon, a New York Times editorial announced that he seemed to lack the basic knowledge taught in high schools, because a rocket obviously needs air to push against. The paper was wrong. A rocket pushes against its own exhaust and works better in a vacuum, which is exactly what Goddard had been saying. On March 16, 1926, on his aunt's farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, Goddard lit the first liquid fuel rocket. It burned gasoline and liquid oxygen. It rose forty one feet, flew for two and a half seconds, and crashed in a cabbage field. It looks like nothing. It was everything. Every launch since, from Apollo to the satellite handling your phone calls, runs on the machine Goddard proved that morning. In July 1969, three days into the flight of Apollo 11, the New York Times printed a short correction. It noted that further investigation had confirmed the work of Isaac Newton, and that a rocket can indeed function in a vacuum. The paper regretted the error. Goddard had been dead for twenty four years.

meta.templateLabel: The Rocket That Throws Itself Away

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The rocket equation: speed depends on exhaust speed and mass ratio
Reaching orbit costs about 9.5 km per second of speed
Hydrogen and oxygen exhaust leaves at about 4.5 km per second
Payload is only a few percent of liftoff weight
Saturn V: about 3,000 tons on the pad, 140 tons to orbit
No single stage rocket has ever reached orbit with a payload
A Falcon 9 booster first landed in December 2015

blocks.prompt: The Tyranny of the Rocket Equation
blocks.text: Every rocket that has ever flown, and every rocket that ever will, obeys a single line of math written in 1903 by a deaf Russian schoolteacher named Konstantin Tsiolkovsky. Engineers still call it the rocket equation, and they often add a second word to the phrase. They call it the tyranny of the rocket equation, because the math is not merely strict. It is cruel. The equation says something that sounds harmless. The speed a rocket can gain depends on two things: how fast it hurls its exhaust out the back, and the ratio between its full weight and its empty weight. The trap is buried in that word ratio. The relationship is not a straight line. It is a curve that bends upward, brutally. Wanting a little more speed does not cost a little more fuel. It costs a multiple. Work the numbers and the problem shows its teeth. To reach orbit, a rocket needs to gain roughly nine and a half kilometers per second, once you pay the tolls that gravity and air resistance charge on the way up. The best chemical exhaust anyone has ever managed, burning hydrogen with oxygen, leaves the nozzle at about four and a half kilometers per second. The equation takes those two numbers and returns a verdict: the rocket on the pad must be roughly eight times heavier than the rocket that arrives. Almost everything you are looking at when you watch a launch is propellant. The metal is a skin stretched around it. The payload, the actual reason for the whole enterprise, is a few percent at the tip. A Saturn V weighed about three thousand tons standing still and delivered around one hundred forty tons to orbit. Staging is the engineer's answer, and it is an admission of defeat as much as a solution. You cannot beat the exponent, so you cheat it. Burn a tank dry, then throw the tank away before the next engine lights, and the ratio resets in your favor. Every rocket that has reached orbit has done this. Not one single stage vehicle has ever carried a useful payload up and stayed in one piece. Which produced an absurdity that lasted sixty years. The most expensive machine on the pad was destroyed on every flight. Imagine scrapping an airliner after one trip to Denver and you have the economics of spaceflight for most of its history. Everyone could see the waste. The problem was that landing a booster requires saving fuel to slow it down, and saving fuel means carrying fuel, and carrying fuel is precisely what the equation punishes. Reuse looked like it might cost more than it saved. In December 2015, a Falcon 9 first stage came back to Cape Canaveral, lit its engines against its own fall, and set itself down on a concrete circle. Fifteen months later, that kind of booster flew a second mission. The equation had not changed and never will. What changed was the willingness to spend part of the payload buying the booster back. That trade is now routine, and it is the reason the price of a kilogram in orbit has fallen further in a decade than in the fifty years before it.
